q: A centrifugal clutch, as used in the drives of workshop machines and equipment, is a clutch which:

options.A: Engages automatically as the speed rises, spring-held shoes being thrown outwards by centrifugal force to press against the inside of a drum
options.B: Is engaged and disengaged only by a hand lever worked by the operator
options.C: Transmits power in one direction only and slips in the other
options.D: Connects two shafts permanently and cannot be disengaged while running

e: A centrifugal clutch engages automatically as speed rises, because spring-held shoes are thrown outwards by centrifugal force to press against the inside of a drum.

q: A ratchet and pawl arrangement, as used in the feed mechanisms of workshop machines, consists of:

options.A: A toothed wheel driven continuously in both directions by a crank
options.B: A wheel and a pivoted block which together convert rotary motion into straight-line motion
options.C: A wheel with inclined teeth and a pivoted pawl engaging the teeth, so that the wheel can turn in one direction only and is prevented from turning back
options.D: A pair of gears which mesh only when the machine is stopped

e: A ratchet and pawl has a wheel with inclined teeth and a pivoted pawl engaging them, so the wheel can turn in one direction only and is prevented from turning back.

q: A ball valve, as fitted on the pipes of a workshop, is a valve in which:

options.A: A wedge-shaped gate is raised or lowered across the passage
options.B: Flow is controlled by a spherical plug with a hole through it, a quarter turn of which brings the hole in line with the pipe to open the valve or across it to close it
options.C: A disc on a spindle is pressed on to a seat in the body of the valve
options.D: Flow is allowed in one direction only and is stopped in the reverse direction

e: In a ball valve flow is controlled by a spherical plug with a hole through it; a quarter turn brings the hole in line with the pipe to open it or across it to close it.

q: A butterfly valve, as fitted on the pipes of a workshop, is a valve in which:

options.A: A ball with a hole through it turns inside the body of the valve
options.B: A long tapered needle moves in and out of a small seat
options.C: A gate slides across the bore of the pipe
options.D: A disc mounted on a spindle across the bore turns edge-on to the flow to open the valve and face-on to the flow to close it

e: In a butterfly valve a disc mounted on a spindle across the bore turns edge-on to the flow to open the valve and face-on to the flow to close it.

q: A needle valve, as fitted on the pipes and equipment of a workshop, is a valve which:

options.A: Has a long, finely tapered needle point moving in a small seat, so that it gives very fine and precise control of a small flow
options.B: Has a spherical plug for quick opening and closing of large pipes
options.C: Allows flow in one direction only
options.D: Opens automatically whenever the pressure in the pipe rises too high

e: A needle valve has a long, finely tapered needle moving in a small seat, so it gives very fine and precise control of a small flow.

q: Under splash lubrication, as used for the machines and engines handled in a workshop:

options.A: Oil is supplied to the parts drop by drop from an oil cup by gravity
options.B: Oil is forced to all the bearings by a pump under pressure
options.C: The moving parts dip into the oil contained in a sump and throw it up as a splash over the surfaces to be lubricated
options.D: A loose ring resting on the shaft carries oil up from a well to the bearing

e: Under splash lubrication the moving parts dip into oil in a sump and throw it up as a splash over the surfaces to be lubricated.

q: Priming of a centrifugal pump, as used in a workshop, means:

options.A: Painting the pump casing with a coat of primer before it is put into use
options.B: Filling the pump casing and the suction pipe completely with the liquid to be pumped, so as to remove all air, before the pump is started
options.C: Running the pump at a low speed for some time when it is first started
options.D: Filling the delivery pipe with liquid from the discharge side

e: Priming a centrifugal pump means filling its casing and suction pipe completely with the liquid to be pumped, removing all air, before the pump is started.

q: A footstep bearing, as used in the machinery of a workshop, is a bearing which:

options.A: Supports a horizontal shaft at its end against axial thrust
options.B: Is fitted in the middle of a long horizontal shaft to prevent it from sagging
options.C: Consists of a collar on the shaft pressing against the face of a bearing block
options.D: Supports the lower end of a vertical shaft, the end of the shaft resting and turning on a flat pivot support at its foot

e: A footstep bearing supports the lower end of a vertical shaft, the end of the shaft resting and turning on a flat pivot support at its foot.

q: A cotter, as used in the assembly work of a workshop, is:

options.A: A flat tapered piece of metal driven through slots in the socket and the rod end, forming a temporary joint between two rods carrying axial loads
options.B: A split pin passed through a nut and bolt to prevent the nut from slackening
options.C: A piece of metal fitted partly in a shaft and partly in a hub to prevent relative rotation
options.D: A pin used for locating two parts of an assembly accurately together

e: A cotter is a flat tapered piece of metal driven through slots in the socket and rod end, forming a temporary joint between two rods carrying axial loads; it is not a key or a split pin.

q: Shaving, as carried out on a press in a workshop, is an operation in which:

options.A: A blank of the required shape is cut out of the sheet in one stroke
options.B: The edge of the sheet is bent over to form a rim
options.C: A very thin layer is removed from the edges of a part already blanked or pierced, in order to obtain smooth, square and accurate edges
options.D: A shallow raised design is formed on the surface of the sheet

e: Shaving removes a very thin layer from the edges of a part already blanked or pierced, in order to obtain smooth, square and accurate edges.

q: Curling, as carried out in the sheet-metal work of a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Cutting the sheet along a straight line by a shearing action
options.B: Forming the edge of a hollow sheet-metal article into a round roll or bead, to strengthen the edge and remove its sharpness
options.C: Joining two edges of the sheet by folding them together
options.D: Stretching the sheet over a form to give it a curved shape

e: Curling forms the edge of a hollow sheet-metal article into a round roll or bead, which strengthens the edge and removes its sharpness.

q: Perforating, as carried out on a press in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Cutting out the outline of a component from the sheet
options.B: Making a single hole in the sheet with a punch and die
options.C: Bending the sheet along a line to a required angle
options.D: Punching a large number of holes in a pattern in the sheet in one operation, as in the making of perforated sheets

e: Perforating is punching a large number of holes in a pattern in the sheet in one press operation, as in making perforated sheets; a single hole is piercing.

q: Flanging, as carried out in the sheet-metal and press work of a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Bending the edge of a sheet or part to form a flange or rim, for stiffening it or for joining it to another part
options.B: Rolling the edge of the sheet back on itself and pressing it flat
options.C: Cutting a slit in the sheet without removing any material
options.D: Interlocking the folded edges of two sheets to form a seam

e: Flanging is bending the edge of a sheet or part to form a flange or rim, for stiffening it or for joining it to another part.

q: Austenite, as the term is used for the structure of steels handled in a workshop, is:

options.A: The name given to pure iron at ordinary temperatures
options.B: A hard compound of iron and carbon found in cast iron
options.C: The solid solution of carbon in gamma iron, having a face-centred cubic structure, which exists at high temperatures and from which the other structures of steel form on cooling
options.D: A layered mixture of two constituents formed on the slow cooling of steel

e: Austenite is the solid solution of carbon in gamma iron with a face-centred cubic structure, existing at high temperatures and from which other steel structures form on cooling.

q: Cementite, as the term is used for the structure of steels and cast irons handled in a workshop, is:

options.A: The form in which carbon occurs as soft flakes in grey cast iron
options.B: Iron carbide, the very hard and brittle compound of iron and carbon present in steels and white cast iron
options.C: The soft and ductile constituent consisting of almost pure iron
options.D: A mixture of iron and iron carbide formed at the eutectoid temperature

e: Cementite is iron carbide, the very hard and brittle compound of iron and carbon present in steels and in white cast iron.

q: Killed steel, as the term is used for the steel handled in a workshop, is steel which:

options.A: Has been hardened throughout by heating and quenching in water
options.B: Has been cast into moulds and allowed to solidify with a vigorous evolution of gas
options.C: Contains a large proportion of impurities removed by repeated melting
options.D: Has been fully deoxidised before casting, so that it solidifies quietly in the mould without any evolution of gas

e: Killed steel has been fully deoxidised before casting, so it solidifies quietly in the mould without any evolution of gas.

q: Decarburisation of a steel component in a workshop is:

options.A: The loss of carbon from the surface layer of the steel during heating in an oxidising atmosphere, leaving a soft and weak skin
options.B: The addition of carbon to the surface layer of the steel during heating
options.C: The formation of a layer of oxide scale on the surface of the steel
options.D: The cracking of the surface of the steel due to very rapid cooling

e: Decarburisation is the loss of carbon from the surface layer of steel during heating in an oxidising atmosphere, leaving a soft and weak skin.

q: A muffle furnace, as used for the heat treatment work of a workshop, is a furnace in which:

options.A: The metal is melted in a crucible placed inside the furnace
options.B: Air is blown in through openings near the bottom to burn the fuel
options.C: The work is heated inside a closed refractory chamber (muffle) which separates it from the flame and the gases of combustion, giving clean and controlled heating
options.D: The charge is melted by an electric arc struck between electrodes

e: In a muffle furnace the work is heated inside a closed refractory chamber, the muffle, which separates it from the flame and combustion gases, giving clean and controlled heating.

q: The heat-affected zone of a welded joint made in a workshop is:

options.A: The pool of metal which is actually melted during welding
options.B: The portion of the parent metal next to the weld which is not melted but whose structure and properties are changed by the heat of welding
options.C: The layer of slag formed over the surface of the weld
options.D: The portion of the parent metal which is too far from the weld to be affected in any way

e: The heat-affected zone is the portion of parent metal next to the weld that is not melted but whose structure and properties are changed by the heat of welding.

q: An arc strike, as the term is used in the welding work of a workshop, is:

options.A: A shower of small droplets of metal thrown out around the weld
options.B: A depression left at the end of a weld where the arc was broken
options.C: The deflection of the welding arc from its intended path by magnetic effects
options.D: A small accidentally melted and hardened spot on the surface of the parent metal outside the weld, caused by the arc being struck there momentarily

e: An arc strike is a small accidentally melted and hardened spot on the parent metal outside the weld, caused by the arc being struck there momentarily.

q: An economiser fitted to a boiler in a workshop is a device which:

options.A: Heats the feed water before it enters the boiler, by using the waste heat of the outgoing flue gases, thereby saving fuel
options.B: Raises the temperature of the steam after it leaves the boiler
options.C: Forces feed water into the boiler against the boiler pressure
options.D: Separates the steam from the water in the boiler drum

e: An economiser heats the boiler feed water before it enters the boiler by using the waste heat of the outgoing flue gases, thereby saving fuel.

q: A superheater fitted to a boiler in a workshop is a device which:

options.A: Heats the feed water by means of the exhaust steam
options.B: Stores the steam produced by the boiler for use at peak load
options.C: Further heats the steam already formed in the boiler, raising its temperature above the saturation temperature at that pressure
options.D: Condenses the exhaust steam back into water for re-use in the boiler

e: A superheater further heats steam already formed in the boiler, raising its temperature above the saturation temperature at that pressure.

q: A fishbone diagram (cause-and-effect diagram), as used in the quality work of a workshop, is a diagram which:

options.A: Shows the measurements of a product arranged as bars according to their frequency
options.B: Shows the causes of rejections arranged in the order of their importance
options.C: Plots the measurements of a process in the order in which they are taken, with control limits
options.D: Displays a problem as the head and groups all its possible causes, arranged under main cause headings, as the bones, so that the root cause can be traced

e: A fishbone diagram displays a problem as the head and groups all its possible causes under main cause headings as the bones, so the root cause can be traced.

q: Under HML analysis, as applied to the material held for workshop use, the items are classified according to:

options.A: The rate at which the items are consumed in the workshop
options.B: The criticality of the items for the working of the workshop
options.C: The total annual value of the consumption of the items
options.D: The unit price of the items, the items being grouped as high, medium and low in unit price

e: Under HML analysis stores items are classified by unit price into high, medium and low price groups, unlike ABC analysis which uses annual consumption value.

q: The carrying cost of an item of material held in stock for a workshop means:

options.A: The price paid to the supplier for purchasing the item
options.B: The cost incurred in placing one order for the item
options.C: The cost of holding the item in stock, comprising storage and insurance charges, deterioration and obsolescence, and the interest on the capital locked up in the stock
options.D: The loss suffered when an item is not in stock at the time it is required

e: Carrying cost is the cost of holding an item in stock, comprising storage and insurance charges, deterioration and obsolescence, and interest on the capital locked up in the stock.

q: In the costing of a workshop, overheads are said to be under-absorbed when:

options.A: The amount of overhead recovered into jobs by applying the absorption rate is greater than the overhead actually incurred
options.B: The amount of overhead recovered into jobs by applying the absorption rate is less than the overhead actually incurred
options.C: The amount of overhead recovered into jobs is exactly equal to the overhead actually incurred
options.D: No overhead at all has been charged to the jobs completed during the period

e: Overheads are under-absorbed when the amount recovered into jobs by applying the absorption rate is less than the overhead actually incurred in workshop costing.

q: In the costing of a workshop, overheads are said to be over-absorbed when:

options.A: The amount of overhead charged to jobs is less than the overhead actually incurred
options.B: The amount of overhead charged to jobs is exactly equal to the overhead actually incurred
options.C: The amount of overhead charged to jobs is more than the overhead actually incurred
options.D: The overhead actually incurred during the period is nil

e: Overheads are over-absorbed when the amount charged to jobs by applying the absorption rate is more than the overhead actually incurred.

q: A supplementary rate in workshop costing is a rate which is used to:

options.A: Distribute the difference between the overhead absorbed and the overhead actually incurred over the jobs of the period
options.B: Fix the selling price of an article manufactured in the workshop for an outside party
options.C: Recover the direct material cost of a job in advance of its completion
options.D: Replace the predetermined absorption rate for all jobs of the following year

e: A supplementary rate is used to distribute the difference between overhead absorbed and overhead actually incurred over the jobs of the period.

q: The machine hour rate, as a method of absorbing workshop overheads, is a rate which is:

options.A: Worked out for each worker separately on the basis of the hours he is present in the shop
options.B: Obtained by dividing the total wages of the shop by the total machine hours of the shop
options.C: Applied only to jobs on which no machine work has been done at all
options.D: Worked out for each machine or group of machines by dividing the overheads of the machine by the number of hours it is expected to work

e: The machine hour rate is worked out for each machine or group of machines by dividing the overheads of the machine by the number of hours it is expected to work.

q: Under the first-in-first-out method of pricing material issued from a workshop store, an issue is priced at:

options.A: The price of the most recent lot of the material received into the store
options.B: The average price of all the lots of the material in stock
options.C: The price of the earliest lot of the material still in stock, lots being exhausted in the order in which they were received
options.D: The price at which the material could be replaced in the market on the date of issue

e: Under FIFO, stores issues are priced at the price of the earliest lot still in stock, lots being exhausted in the order in which they were received.

q: Under the last-in-first-out method of pricing material issued from a workshop store, an issue is priced at:

options.A: The price of the most recent lot of the material received, that lot being treated as issued first
options.B: The price of the earliest lot of the material received into the store
options.C: The standard price fixed for the material for the whole year
options.D: The lowest price at which the material was received during the year

e: Under LIFO, stores issues are priced at the price of the most recent lot received, that lot being treated as issued first.

q: Under a periodic inventory system, as followed for the material of a workshop store:

options.A: A continuous record of receipts, issues and balances is maintained for every item
options.B: The stock of material is ascertained by actual physical counting only at the end of a period, no continuous balance record being kept
options.C: Every item of material is counted and verified every day by an independent verifier
options.D: The balance of material is taken from the bin cards without any physical counting at any time

e: Under a periodic inventory system the stock of material is ascertained by actual physical counting only at the end of a period, with no continuous balance record kept.

q: Under the reciprocal method of reapportioning the costs of the service departments of a workshop:

options.A: Each service department is apportioned to the production departments one after another, without recognising the services it receives from other service departments
options.B: The costs of all service departments are charged wholly to the largest production department
options.C: No service department cost is apportioned to any production department at all
options.D: The services rendered by one service department to another are recognised, the departments being treated as rendering services to each other mutually

e: Under the reciprocal method of reapportionment the services rendered by one service department to another are recognised, the departments being treated as serving each other mutually.

q: Under XYZ analysis, as applied to the material held for workshop use, the items are classified according to:

options.A: The value of the stock of each item held in store (quantity in stock multiplied by its unit price), the items of highest stock value forming the X class, those of medium stock value the Y class and those of lowest stock value the Z class
options.B: The unit price of the items, from the highest-priced to the lowest-priced
options.C: The annual value of consumption of the items
options.D: The source from which the items are procured, whether local or foreign

e: Under XYZ analysis items are classified by the value of stock held, that is quantity in stock multiplied by unit price, X being the highest stock value class and Z the lowest.

q: Continuous stock taking in a workshop store means a system under which:

options.A: The entire store is closed once a year and every item in it is counted at one time
options.B: Only the items suspected of shortage are counted, and that too only on a complaint
options.C: A few items are counted and checked in rotation every day throughout the year, so that each item is verified several times without closing the store
options.D: The stock is verified only when the storekeeper in charge of the store is transferred

e: Continuous stock taking means a few items are counted and checked in rotation every day throughout the year, so each item is verified several times without closing the store.

q: An air vessel fitted to a reciprocating pump used in a workshop serves the purpose of:

options.A: Removing the air dissolved in the liquid before the liquid enters the pump
options.B: Making the flow of liquid in the delivery pipe more continuous and uniform by storing liquid and releasing it during the idle part of the stroke
options.C: Increasing the pressure of the liquid far beyond the pressure the pump can develop
options.D: Filtering out the solid particles suspended in the liquid handled by the pump

e: An air vessel on a reciprocating pump makes delivery flow more continuous and uniform by storing liquid and releasing it during the idle part of the stroke.

q: A p-chart, as used in the quality work of a workshop, is a control chart which is drawn for:

options.A: The average value of a measurable dimension of the components produced
options.B: The number of defects found in each single component inspected
options.C: The total number of components produced in each shift
options.D: The proportion or fraction of defective components in the samples inspected

e: A p-chart is a control chart drawn for the proportion or fraction of defective components in the samples inspected.

q: A c-chart, as used in the quality work of a workshop, is a control chart which is drawn for:

options.A: The number of defects found per unit or per inspection unit, the size of the unit remaining constant
options.B: The fraction of defective components in samples of varying size
options.C: The range of a measurable dimension within each sample
options.D: The average number of components rejected in a month

e: A c-chart is a control chart drawn for the number of defects found per unit or per inspection unit, the size of the unit remaining constant.

q: The 5S system, as practised for organising a workplace in a workshop, stands for a set of steps whose object is to:

options.A: Divide the workers of a shop into five shifts for continuous working
options.B: Keep the workplace orderly and clean by sorting out what is needed, arranging it in place, cleaning, standardising the practice and sustaining the discipline
options.C: Inspect every fifth component produced in the shop for defects
options.D: Replace the five oldest machines of the shop with new machines every year

e: The 5S system keeps the workplace orderly and clean by sorting out what is needed, arranging it in place, cleaning, standardising the practice and sustaining the discipline.

q: A spirit level, as used by the fitters and machinists of a workshop, is an instrument which is used for:

options.A: Measuring the exact angle of an inclined surface in degrees
options.B: Marking centre lines on a job laid on the marking table
options.C: Testing whether a surface is truly horizontal or vertical, by observing the bubble of liquid sealed in a slightly curved glass tube
options.D: Measuring the depth of a blind hole in a component

e: A spirit level tests whether a surface is truly horizontal or vertical by observing the bubble of liquid sealed in a slightly curved glass tube.

q: A small hole gauge, as used in the inspection work of a workshop, is a gauge which is used for:

options.A: Measuring the diameter of small holes, its expanding split end being set in the hole and the size then read with a micrometer
options.B: Checking whether the depth of a small hole is within the prescribed limits
options.C: Measuring the pitch of a small internal thread inside a hole
options.D: Testing the hardness of the material around a small hole

e: A small hole gauge measures the diameter of small holes; its expanding split end is set in the hole and the size is then read with a micrometer.

q: The zero error of a measuring instrument used in a workshop means the error by which:

options.A: The instrument reads a value other than the true value only at the top of its range
options.B: The least count of the instrument differs from the least count marked on it
options.C: The instrument is set right at zero but drifts while a measurement is being taken
options.D: The instrument shows a reading other than zero when it ought to show zero, as when the measuring faces of a micrometer are fully closed

e: Zero error is the error by which an instrument shows a reading other than zero when it ought to show zero, as when the measuring faces of a micrometer are fully closed.

q: An optical flat, as used in the inspection section of a workshop, is used for:

options.A: Grinding the surface of a component to a very fine finish
options.B: Testing the flatness of a surface by the pattern of interference bands formed under it in light
options.C: Measuring the thickness of a thin component directly from its engraved scale
options.D: Holding a component flat on the table of a machine while it is being machined

e: An optical flat is used to test the flatness of a surface by the pattern of interference bands formed under it in light.

q: Surface roughness of a machined surface in a workshop means:

options.A: The fine irregularities of the surface texture, of small spacing, left by the machining process itself
options.B: The widely spaced undulations of the surface caused by deflection of the machine
options.C: The departure of the whole surface from the specified shape or form
options.D: The scratches made on the surface by careless handling after machining

e: Surface roughness means the fine irregularities of surface texture, of small spacing, left by the machining process itself, distinct from waviness and form error.

q: In up milling, also called conventional milling, as carried out on a milling machine in a workshop:

options.A: The cutter and the workpiece move in the same direction at the point of cutting
options.B: The workpiece is held stationary and only the cutter is fed across it
options.C: The workpiece is fed in the direction opposite to the rotation of the cutter at the point of cutting, so that the chip begins with the smallest thickness
options.D: The cutter is fed vertically downwards into the workpiece throughout the cut

e: In up milling or conventional milling the workpiece is fed opposite to the rotation of the cutter at the point of cutting, so the chip begins with the smallest thickness.

q: In climb milling, also called down milling, as carried out on a milling machine in a workshop:

options.A: The workpiece is fed against the direction of rotation of the cutter
options.B: The thickness of the chip is the smallest at the start of the cut and grows gradually
options.C: The cutter rotates in the reverse direction to that used in ordinary milling
options.D: The workpiece is fed in the same direction as the rotation of the cutter at the point of cutting, so that the chip begins with the greatest thickness

e: In climb or down milling the workpiece is fed in the same direction as the rotation of the cutter at the point of cutting, so the chip begins with the greatest thickness.

q: Loading of a grinding wheel, as the term is used in a workshop, means the condition in which:

options.A: The wheel is charged with a fresh layer of abrasive grains on its face
options.B: Particles of the metal being ground become clogged in the spaces between the abrasive grains of the wheel, so that the wheel stops cutting freely
options.C: The wheel is mounted on the spindle with a load heavier than its rated capacity
options.D: The grains of the wheel are worn out completely and the bond alone remains on the face

e: Loading of a grinding wheel is the clogging of the spaces between its abrasive grains with particles of the metal being ground, so the wheel stops cutting freely.

q: The grit size of a grinding wheel used in a workshop refers to:

options.A: The size of the abrasive grains held in the wheel, a coarse grit being used for heavy and soft work and a fine grit for finishing
options.B: The overall diameter and thickness of the wheel as a whole
options.C: The strength with which the bond of the wheel holds its grains
options.D: The number of pores or empty spaces present in the structure of the wheel

e: The grit size of a grinding wheel refers to the size of its abrasive grains, a coarse grit being used for heavy and soft work and a fine grit for finishing.

q: The grade of a grinding wheel used in a workshop refers to:

options.A: The size of the abrasive grains held in the wheel
options.B: The material of the abrasive from which the wheel is made
options.C: The strength with which the bond holds the abrasive grains in the wheel, a hard grade holding the grains more firmly than a soft grade
options.D: The maximum speed at which the wheel is permitted to run

e: The grade of a grinding wheel refers to the strength with which the bond holds the abrasive grains, a hard grade holding the grains more firmly than a soft grade.

q: A cross-cut chisel, also called a cape chisel, as used by the fitters of a workshop, is a chisel which is used for:

options.A: Cutting off the heads of rivets fitted in an assembly
options.B: Chipping a flat surface over a wide area in one pass
options.C: Rounding the corners of a square hole in a plate
options.D: Cutting keyways, grooves and narrow channels in a job, its cutting edge being narrow and slightly wider than the body behind it

e: A cross-cut or cape chisel is used for cutting keyways, grooves and narrow channels, its cutting edge being narrow and slightly wider than the body behind it to prevent sticking.

q: The half nut of a lathe in a workshop is the mechanism which:

options.A: Holds the tailstock of the lathe firmly in position on the bed
options.B: Engages the carriage with the lead screw for cutting threads, the split nut being closed on the screw by a lever when required
options.C: Locks the spindle of the headstock against rotation during tool setting
options.D: Connects the feed rod of the lathe to the apron for ordinary turning feeds

e: The half nut of a lathe engages the carriage with the lead screw for cutting threads, the split nut being closed on the screw by a lever when required.

q: In arc welding carried out in a workshop, the arc length means:

options.A: The distance between the tip of the electrode and the surface of the workpiece across which the arc is maintained
options.B: The total length of the welded joint produced in one run of the electrode
options.C: The length of the electrode consumed in completing one joint
options.D: The distance between the welding machine and the workpiece being welded

e: In arc welding the arc length is the distance between the tip of the electrode and the surface of the workpiece across which the arc is maintained.

q: In direct-current arc welding in a workshop, straight polarity means the arrangement in which:

options.A: The electrode is connected to the positive terminal and the workpiece to the negative terminal
options.B: Both the electrode and the workpiece are connected to the same terminal
options.C: The electrode is connected to the negative terminal and the workpiece to the positive terminal of the supply
options.D: The supply is changed over from one terminal to the other after every pass

e: In direct-current arc welding, straight polarity means the electrode is connected to the negative terminal and the workpiece to the positive terminal of the supply.

q: In direct-current arc welding in a workshop, reverse polarity means the arrangement in which:

options.A: The electrode is connected to the negative terminal and the workpiece to the positive terminal
options.B: Alternating current is used instead of direct current for the welding
options.C: The workpiece is connected to both the terminals of the supply in turn
options.D: The electrode is connected to the positive terminal and the workpiece to the negative terminal of the supply

e: In direct-current arc welding, reverse polarity means the electrode is connected to the positive terminal and the workpiece to the negative terminal of the supply.

q: Malleable iron, as the term is used for the castings handled in a workshop, is iron which is:

options.A: Cast directly in the mould in the form in which it acquires its ductility
options.B: Produced by heat-treating white iron castings for a prolonged period, so that the brittle castings become ductile and can bear shocks
options.C: Obtained by adding a large proportion of steel scrap to grey iron in the cupola
options.D: Rolled into sheets and bars in the same way as wrought iron

e: Malleable iron is produced by heat-treating white iron castings for a prolonged period, so the brittle castings become ductile and can bear shocks.

q: Nodular iron, also called spheroidal graphite iron, as handled in a workshop, is cast iron in which:

options.A: The graphite is present in the form of rounded nodules or spheroids instead of flakes, giving the iron ductility along with strength
options.B: The graphite is present in the form of long thin flakes throughout the metal
options.C: No graphite is present in the metal in any form at all
options.D: The carbon is present wholly in the combined form, making the iron very hard and brittle

e: In nodular or spheroidal graphite iron the graphite is present as rounded nodules or spheroids instead of flakes, giving the iron ductility along with strength.

q: Season cracking, as the term is used for brass articles handled in a workshop, is:

options.A: The cracking of brass articles caused by heating them repeatedly in service
options.B: The surface tarnishing of brass articles exposed to the open air for a long time
options.C: The cracking of cold-worked brass articles under their own internal stresses in an atmosphere containing ammonia
options.D: The breaking of brass castings while they are cooling in the mould itself

e: Season cracking is the cracking of cold-worked brass articles under their own internal stresses in an atmosphere containing ammonia.

q: Hydrogen embrittlement of a steel component handled in a workshop means the condition in which the steel:

options.A: Becomes soft and weak because of the loss of its carbon content
options.B: Rusts rapidly on the surface when stored in a damp shed
options.C: Absorbs sulphur from the furnace gases and becomes brittle when hot
options.D: Loses its ductility and becomes liable to crack because of hydrogen absorbed into it, as during pickling or electroplating of high-strength steel

e: Hydrogen embrittlement is the loss of ductility and liability to crack caused by hydrogen absorbed into steel, as during pickling or electroplating of high-strength steel.

q: Degassing of molten metal in the foundry work of a workshop means:

options.A: The removal of dissolved gases from the molten metal before it is poured, so that blowholes and porosity are prevented in the casting
options.B: The removal of slag floating on the surface of the molten metal in the ladle
options.C: The addition of elements to the molten metal to refine its grain structure
options.D: The escape of the air of the mould through the vents while the metal is being poured

e: Degassing is the removal of dissolved gases from molten metal before pouring, so that blowholes and porosity are prevented in the casting.

q: Rimming steel, as the term is used for the steel handled in a workshop, is steel which:

options.A: Has been fully killed by the addition of deoxidising elements before it is teemed
options.B: Has not been fully deoxidised, so that gases continue to evolve and rimming action goes on while it solidifies in the ingot mould
options.C: Has been cast in a round mould so as to take the shape of a rim
options.D: Is used only for making the rims of the wheels of rolling stock

e: Rimming steel has not been fully deoxidised, so gases continue to evolve and rimming action goes on while it solidifies in the ingot mould.

q: A eutectic, as the term is used for the alloys handled in a workshop, is:

options.A: The alloy of a system which has the highest melting point among all compositions of that system
options.B: A mixture of two metals which do not dissolve in each other in any proportion
options.C: The particular composition of an alloy system which melts and solidifies at a single constant temperature, the lowest in that system
options.D: The solid solution formed when one metal dissolves completely in another

e: A eutectic is the particular composition of an alloy system which melts and solidifies at a single constant temperature, the lowest in that system.

q: A flatter, as used in the smithy work of a workshop, is a tool which is used for:

options.A: Punching round holes in a hot job held on the anvil
options.B: Cutting a hot bar of metal into pieces of the required length
options.C: Drawing out a hot job to a longer length and smaller section
options.D: Finishing and smoothing flat surfaces of a forged job, the tool being placed on the job and struck with a hammer

e: A flatter is used for finishing and smoothing flat surfaces of a forged job; it is placed on the job in the smithy and struck with a hammer.

q: Drop forging, as carried out in a workshop, is the process of:

options.A: Shaping heated metal in closed dies by the repeated blows of a hammer which is raised and dropped on it, the excess metal escaping as flash
options.B: Forging a job by squeezing it slowly in a hydraulic press without any blow
options.C: Casting metal in a metal mould and then trimming the casting to shape
options.D: Dropping a heated job repeatedly from a height to consolidate its metal

e: Drop forging shapes heated metal in closed dies by repeated blows of a hammer raised and dropped on it, the excess metal escaping as flash.

q: In hot-chamber die casting, as carried out for workshop components:

options.A: A measured quantity of molten metal is ladled into a separate cold chamber for every shot made
options.B: The injection mechanism remains immersed in the molten metal itself, the process suiting alloys of low melting point
options.C: The metal is poured into the die by gravity alone, without any pressure on it
options.D: The die is kept hotter than the metal poured into it throughout the casting

e: In hot-chamber die casting the injection mechanism remains immersed in the molten metal itself, so the process suits alloys of low melting point.

q: In cold-chamber die casting, as carried out for workshop components:

options.A: The die is cooled below the freezing point before the metal is poured into it
options.B: The metal is injected into the die while it is still in the solid state
options.C: A measured quantity of molten metal is poured into a separate chamber, which is not immersed in the molten metal, for every shot, the process suiting alloys of higher melting point
options.D: No pressure at all is applied to the metal as it enters the die cavity

e: In cold-chamber die casting a measured quantity of molten metal is poured into a separate chamber, not immersed in the molten metal, for every shot, suiting alloys of higher melting point.

q: Slip in a belt drive of a workshop machine means:

options.A: The slipping of the belt sideways off the face of the pulley while running
options.B: The gradual lengthening of the belt in service because of its elasticity
options.C: The movement of the belt on the pulley caused by the vibration of the machine
options.D: The relative motion between the belt and the surface of the pulley because the grip between them is insufficient, reducing the velocity ratio of the drive

e: Slip in a belt drive is the relative motion between the belt and the pulley surface because grip between them is insufficient, which reduces the velocity ratio of the drive.

q: A dog clutch, as used in the machinery of a workshop, is a clutch in which:

options.A: Square teeth or jaws on the two halves engage with corresponding slots, giving a positive drive without slip, engagement being possible only at rest or at very low speed
options.B: Two smooth conical surfaces are pressed together and drive by friction alone
options.C: Friction blocks fly outwards under speed and grip the inside of a drum
options.D: A coil of wire grips the drum progressively as the load on it increases

e: A dog clutch has square teeth or jaws on its two halves engaging with corresponding slots, giving a positive drive without slip, engageable only at rest or very low speed.

q: A taper roller bearing, as used in the machinery of a workshop, is a bearing which:

options.A: Can carry radial load only and no end thrust in any direction
options.B: Has tapered rollers running between tapered races, so that it can carry radial and thrust loads together
options.C: Has no rolling elements at all and works by plain sliding contact
options.D: Is made wholly of plain bushes pressed into the housing of the machine

e: A taper roller bearing has tapered rollers running between tapered races, so it can carry radial and thrust loads together.

q: Under ring-oiling lubrication, as used for the bearings of workshop machines:

options.A: Oil is forced to the bearing continuously by a pump driven from the machine itself
options.B: The bearing is packed once with grease and is not oiled again in service
options.C: A loose ring rests on the journal and dips into an oil reservoir below, carrying oil up to the journal as it turns with it
options.D: Oil reaches the bearing only by the splashing of the parts moving in the oil sump

e: Under ring-oiling a loose ring rests on the journal and dips into an oil reservoir below, carrying oil up to the journal as it turns with it.

q: A reciprocating pump, as used in a workshop, is a pump in which:

options.A: A rotating impeller throws the liquid outwards by centrifugal action
options.B: A screw rotating inside a casing pushes the liquid steadily along the axis
options.C: A jet of steam is used to lift the liquid without any moving part in the pump
options.D: A piston or plunger moving to and fro in a cylinder draws in the liquid on one stroke and forces it out on the other

e: A reciprocating pump works by a piston or plunger moving to and fro in a cylinder, drawing liquid in on one stroke and forcing it out on the other.

q: An autocollimator, as used for precision checking in a workshop, is an optical instrument employed mainly for:

options.A: Measuring the length of a workpiece directly against a graduated scale
options.B: Detecting and measuring very small angular displacements or tilts of a flat reflecting surface
options.C: Magnifying the profile of a small component for comparison with a template
options.D: Measuring the pressure of the air escaping from a gauging jet

e: An autocollimator is an optical instrument used mainly for detecting and measuring very small angular displacements or tilts of a flat reflecting surface.

q: A profile projector (optical projector) used in the inspection section of a workshop serves mainly to:

options.A: Project the drawings of a component on the notice board of the shop
options.B: Harden the surface of small components by a beam of light
options.C: Throw a greatly magnified shadow image of a small component on a screen, so that its profile can be compared with a standard template
options.D: Measure the temperature of a heated component from a distance

e: A profile projector throws a greatly magnified shadow image of a small component on a screen, so its profile can be compared with a standard template.

q: A coordinate measuring machine (CMM) in a modern workshop is used for:

options.A: Determining the dimensions of a component by probing points on its surfaces and computing the measurements along three mutually perpendicular axes
options.B: Coordinating the movement of workpieces between two machine tools
options.C: Measuring the coordinates of machines laid out on the shop floor
options.D: Checking the coordinates of holes marked out on a surface plate by hand

e: A coordinate measuring machine determines dimensions by probing points on the surfaces of a component and computing measurements along three mutually perpendicular axes.

q: A screw thread micrometer, as used in a workshop, differs from an ordinary outside micrometer in that it is fitted with a pointed spindle and a V-shaped anvil, and it measures directly:

options.A: The major diameter of the threaded part
options.B: The minor diameter of the threaded part
options.C: The length of the threaded portion of the part
options.D: The pitch diameter (effective diameter) of the screw thread

e: A screw thread micrometer has a pointed spindle and a V-shaped anvil and measures directly the pitch diameter, also called the effective diameter, of a screw thread.

q: A depth micrometer used in a workshop is an instrument employed for measuring accurately:

options.A: The pitch of a screw thread
options.B: The depth of holes, slots, shoulders and recesses in a component
options.C: The thickness of a workpiece at a point deep inside a bore only
options.D: The distance between two opposite faces of a long shaft

e: A depth micrometer is employed for measuring accurately the depth of holes, slots, shoulders and recesses in a component.

q: Abbe's principle, which is followed in the design and use of precision measuring instruments in a workshop, states that, to obtain the most accurate measurement:

options.A: The instrument must always be used at the standard room temperature
options.B: The workpiece must be supported at its Airy points during measurement
options.C: The line of measurement and the axis of the measuring scale should lie along the same straight line
options.D: The measuring faces of the instrument must be hardened and lapped

e: Abbe principle states that for the most accurate measurement the line of measurement and the axis of the measuring scale should lie along the same straight line.

q: A fly press, as installed in the fitting and sheet-metal shops of a workshop, is:

options.A: A hand-operated screw press in which a heavy flywheel and ball weights drive the ram down through a screw, used for small punching, blanking and forming work
options.B: A power press in which the ram is driven by a crank and a flywheel
options.C: A press in which the ram is worked by compressed air
options.D: A hydraulic press used for pressing wheels on axles

e: A fly press is a hand-operated screw press in which a heavy flywheel and ball weights drive the ram down through a screw, used for small punching, blanking and forming work.

q: A press brake, as used in the sheet-metal shop of a workshop, is a machine employed for:

options.A: Slowing down the ram of a power press at the end of its stroke
options.B: Cutting sheets to size by a pair of shear blades
options.C: Punching a series of holes along the edge of a sheet
options.D: Bending sheet metal along a straight line, between a narrow punch and a matching die

e: A press brake is a machine employed for bending sheet metal along a straight line between a narrow punch and a matching die.

q: An automatic lathe, as used for the mass production of small turned components in a workshop, differs from a centre lathe mainly in that:

options.A: It works only on bar stock and cannot work on castings
options.B: Once it is set, the whole machining cycle, including the feeding of the bar and the changing of tools, is carried out automatically and the operator only loads the machine and inspects the output
options.C: Its spindle is driven by an individual motor instead of a belt
options.D: It can cut screw threads without the use of a lead screw

e: An automatic lathe differs from a centre lathe in that, once set, the whole machining cycle including bar feeding and tool changing is automatic and the operator only loads and inspects.

q: In a pantograph milling arrangement used in a workshop, the profile required on the workpiece is produced by:

options.A: A formed cutter whose own shape is the shape to be produced
options.B: Interchangeable cams fitted on the spindle of the machine
options.C: A tracer which is guided over a template or model, its movement being reproduced in a reduced or enlarged ratio by the cutter
options.D: A dividing head which indexes the workpiece after every cut

e: In pantograph milling a tracer is guided over a template or model and its movement is reproduced in a reduced or enlarged ratio by the cutter on the workpiece.

q: A circular saw (cold saw), as used for cutting material in a workshop, cuts the stock by means of:

options.A: A rotating toothed disc blade which is fed into the work
options.B: A thin band blade running continuously over two pulleys
options.C: A reciprocating blade drawn back and forth across the work
options.D: An abrasive wheel which grinds its way through the section

e: A circular or cold saw cuts stock by means of a rotating toothed disc blade which is fed into the work.

q: A machining centre, as installed in a modern workshop, is a machine tool which is characterised by:

options.A: A centre lathe fitted with a number of additional attachments
options.B: A machine on which all the machines of a shop are centrally controlled by one operator
options.C: A milling machine provided with an indexing dividing head
options.D: A numerically controlled machine which can perform several operations, such as milling, drilling and boring, on a workpiece in one setting, with automatic changing of tools from a magazine

e: A machining centre is a numerically controlled machine that can perform several operations such as milling, drilling and boring in one setting, with automatic tool changing from a magazine.

q: A pneumatic gauge (air gauge), as used for checking components in a workshop, takes its measurement from:

options.A: The deflection of a pointer moved by a rack and pinion
options.B: The change in the pressure or rate of flow of compressed air escaping from a gauging jet, as the clearance between the jet and the workpiece surface varies
options.C: The expansion of a column of mercury in a glass tube
options.D: The variation in the electrical resistance of a strain element

e: A pneumatic or air gauge takes its measurement from the change in pressure or rate of flow of compressed air escaping from a gauging jet as the clearance to the workpiece varies.

q: A chaser, as used on a lathe in a workshop, is a tool employed for:

options.A: Cutting a thread afresh on a plain cylindrical bar in a single pass
options.B: Holding a die for cutting an external thread by hand
options.C: Truing up, sizing and finishing a screw thread which has already been roughed out, its teeth corresponding to the pitch of the thread
options.D: Chasing out a damaged keyway in a shaft

e: A chaser is used for truing up, sizing and finishing a screw thread already roughed out, its teeth corresponding to the pitch of the thread.

q: A transfer caliper, as used by a fitter in a workshop, is provided with an auxiliary arm or leg so that:

options.A: The setting of the caliper is retained when it is withdrawn from a recess or other position from which it cannot be removed directly, and the measurement can then be read or compared
options.B: The measurement can be transferred from one workpiece to another without a scale
options.C: It can be used both as an inside and as an outside caliper
options.D: It can measure the transfer of a dimension from a drawing to the work

e: A transfer caliper has an auxiliary arm or leg so its setting is retained when withdrawn from a recess it cannot be removed from directly, and the measurement can then be read.

q: A hypoeutectoid steel, as the term is used for the steels handled in a workshop, is a steel whose carbon content is:

options.A: Exactly equal to the eutectoid composition
options.B: Higher than that of cast iron
options.C: Nil, the steel being practically pure iron
options.D: Less than the eutectoid composition, so that its structure contains free ferrite along with pearlite

e: A hypoeutectoid steel has carbon content less than the eutectoid composition, so its structure contains free ferrite along with pearlite.

q: A hypereutectoid steel, as the term is used for the steels handled in a workshop, is a steel whose carbon content is:

options.A: Less than the eutectoid composition
options.B: More than the eutectoid composition, so that its structure contains free cementite along with pearlite
options.C: The same as that of a eutectoid steel
options.D: More than that of a high-carbon cast iron

e: A hypereutectoid steel has carbon content more than the eutectoid composition, so its structure contains free cementite along with pearlite.

q: Precipitation hardening (age hardening) of a non-ferrous alloy component in a workshop is a treatment in which hardness and strength are developed by:

options.A: Quenching the component in oil from a high temperature
options.B: Hammering the component while it is cold, so that it work-hardens
options.C: Heating the component to dissolve the alloying element, quenching it to retain a supersaturated solution, and then ageing it so that fine particles precipitate within the structure
options.D: Packing the component in carbon and holding it at a high temperature for several hours

e: Precipitation or age hardening develops hardness by dissolving the alloying element, quenching to retain a supersaturated solution, and ageing so fine particles precipitate within the structure.

q: Ledeburite, as the term is used in the metallurgy of the cast irons handled in a workshop foundry, is:

options.A: The eutectic mixture of austenite and cementite which forms on the solidification of cast iron
options.B: The name given to the graphite flakes present in grey cast iron
options.C: A slag-like impurity which floats to the top of the molten metal in the cupola
options.D: The hard skin formed on the surface of a chilled casting

e: Ledeburite is the eutectic mixture of austenite and cementite which forms on the solidification of cast iron.

q: Under a process layout of the machines in a workshop:

options.A: Machines are arranged in the sequence of the operations to be performed on one product
options.B: Machines performing the same kind of operation are grouped together in one shop or bay, and a job travels from group to group as its operations require
options.C: The product remains stationary and the machines are brought to it
options.D: Machines are arranged in cells, each cell completing a family of similar components

e: Under a process layout machines performing the same kind of operation are grouped together in one shop or bay, and a job travels from group to group as its operations require.

q: Under a product layout (line layout) of the machines in a workshop:

options.A: Machines performing the same operation are grouped together department-wise
options.B: The product is built at one fixed place and all facilities are brought to it
options.C: Machines are laid out in the order of the departments which own them
options.D: Machines are arranged in the sequence of the operations required for a particular product, which moves from machine to machine along the line

e: Under a product or line layout machines are arranged in the sequence of operations required for a particular product, which moves from machine to machine along the line.

q: A fixed-position layout is adopted in a workshop for an article such as a complete locomotive or coach under construction, because:

options.A: The machines required are too heavy to be moved about the shop
options.B: The article is produced in a continuous flow from shop to shop
options.C: The article itself remains at one place, and men, materials, tools and equipment are brought to it, it being too large or heavy to move from station to station
options.D: The position of the machines in the shop cannot be changed once they are installed

e: A fixed-position layout is used because the article itself remains at one place and men, materials, tools and equipment are brought to it, it being too large or heavy to move.

q: In acceptance sampling of the components received or produced in a workshop, the Acceptable Quality Level (AQL) means:

options.A: The maximum percentage of defective pieces in a lot which can be regarded as satisfactory as an average of the process, for the purpose of sampling inspection
options.B: The percentage of defective pieces which will be rejected in every case
options.C: The level of quality at which the whole lot is inspected piece by piece
options.D: The percentage of defective pieces found in a sample, whatever the size of the lot

e: The Acceptable Quality Level is the maximum percentage of defective pieces in a lot which can be regarded as satisfactory as an average of the process for sampling inspection.

q: The process capability of a machining process in a workshop refers to:

options.A: The maximum rate at which the process can turn out components in a shift
options.B: The ability of the process, when it is working under control, to turn out components consistently within the specified limits of size
options.C: The capacity of the machine employed on the process, expressed in horsepower
options.D: The proportion of the components of a batch which is actually inspected

e: Process capability is the ability of a process, when working under control, to turn out components consistently within the specified limits of size.

q: A quality audit, as carried out in connection with the quality system of a workshop, consists of:

options.A: Inspecting every finished component before it is passed for use
options.B: Checking the cost of the rejections made in the shop over a period
options.C: Auditing the accounts of the inspection department of the workshop
options.D: A systematic and independent examination to determine whether the quality activities and their results comply with the arrangements planned for them and whether those arrangements are being implemented effectively

e: A quality audit is a systematic and independent examination to determine whether quality activities and their results comply with the planned arrangements and whether those arrangements are implemented effectively.

q: In workshop costing, shutdown costs are those costs which:

options.A: Are incurred in dismantling a plant which is being permanently closed down
options.B: Represent the cost of shutting a work order on which no further work is to be done
options.C: Continue to be incurred, or are specifically incurred, during a period when the plant or shop is temporarily shut down and no production takes place, such as rent, insurance and the upkeep of the idle plant
options.D: Are charged when a machine is stopped for its routine daily maintenance

e: Shutdown costs are costs which continue to be incurred, or are specifically incurred, during a temporary shutdown with no production, such as rent, insurance and upkeep of idle plant.

q: In costing, a relevant cost for a decision about a workshop job is a cost which:

options.A: Is a future cost which will be affected by the decision, differing between the alternatives under consideration
options.B: Has already been incurred in the past on similar jobs
options.C: Is common to all the alternatives under consideration
options.D: Is recorded in the cost accounts of the workshop for the previous year

e: A relevant cost is a future cost which will be affected by the decision and differs between the alternatives under consideration; past and common costs are not relevant.

q: In a cost sheet of a workshop, the cost of sales of the output is arrived at by:

options.A: Adding the selling and distribution overheads to the prime cost of the output
options.B: Taking the cost of production, adjusting it for the opening and closing stocks of finished work, and adding the selling and distribution overheads
options.C: Deducting the selling and distribution overheads from the factory cost
options.D: Taking the works cost adjusted for the opening and closing stocks of finished work, without any selling overheads

e: Cost of sales is arrived at by taking the cost of production, adjusting it for opening and closing stocks of finished work, and adding selling and distribution overheads.

q: Idle capacity of a workshop, as the term is used in costing, means:

options.A: The capacity of the machines which are awaiting repairs in the shop
options.B: The difference between the installed capacity and the licensed capacity of the shop
options.C: The capacity lost on account of the idle time of the workers alone
options.D: That part of the normal (practical) capacity of the shop which remains unutilised in a period, the fixed cost relating to it being a loss of the period rather than a part of the cost of the work done

e: Idle capacity is that part of the normal or practical capacity of the shop which remains unutilised in a period, and its fixed cost is a loss of the period, not part of the cost of work done.

q: Materials requirement planning (MRP), as used for production control in a workshop, is a system under which:

options.A: Materials are indented on the stores depot only when the shop stock is fully exhausted
options.B: The requirements of materials and components for the planned output are worked out from the production programme and the composition of each product, and are phased over the periods in which they will actually be needed, allowing for stocks in hand and lead times
options.C: The maximum and minimum stock levels of every item are fixed by the stores depot
options.D: Materials are issued to the shops against a monthly quota fixed by the headquarters office

e: Under materials requirement planning, material and component requirements are worked out from the production programme and the composition of each product and phased over the periods needed, allowing for stocks in hand and lead times.
